source.title: Learning to Learn From Noisy Labeled Data
source.authors: Junnan Li; Yong-Kang Wong; Qi Zhao; Mohan Kankanhalli

record.tranche_reason: Tests performance under varying label-noise rates, but uses a meta-learning noise-tolerant training method and reports classification accuracy rather than the original random-label fitting measure.
record.gate_note: The paper varies synthetic symmetric and asymmetric label-noise rates and reports test accuracy. It does not report fitting a completely random labeling, test error at chance, training time versus clean-label training, or results on unstructured inputs. The training-accuracy curve is described in the text but its values are available only in a figure.
record.test_reason: The authors' conventional cross-entropy baseline measures how clean-test accuracy changes with synthetic label corruption, bearing on V4's degradation component. The proposed noise-tolerant method is not itself a test of standard networks' random-label fitting. Neither perfect training fit across noise rates nor the fully random endpoint is established.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that MLNT and iterative training improve noisy-label classification on CIFAR-10 and Clothing1M. They explicitly report an exception to outperforming competing methods at 50% asymmetric CIFAR-10 noise.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a meta-learning update with synthetic neighbor-transferred labels, teacher consistency, and iterative filtering; this is not the original random-label memorization experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported test accuracy varies with noise rate and noise type; on CIFAR-10 the paper reports an exception at 50% asymmetric noise.

fits_no_version.finding: MLNT improves test accuracy relative to conventional cross entropy, and iterative filtering usually improves it further.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A meta-learning consistency objective and iterative filtering can improve generalization from noisy labels.

record.problems: The results concern a noise-tolerant method and test accuracy under selected synthetic noise rates, not the original random-label fitting claim. Training accuracy values appear only in a plot; uncertainty is not reported for all baseline values.
record.rows_left_out: No other table rows extracted: the MLNT student and teacher test-accuracy results are competing noise-tolerant methods and do not establish whether standard networks fit random labels. Figure 3's training-accuracy curve is figure-only and has no stated numerical values.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters relative to clean-label training.
Training-time ratios and convergence slowing as corruption increases. Faster early learning by MLNT than cross entropy compares methods rather than clean and random labels.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit across corruption rates and the fully random endpoint. Symmetric noise stops at r=0.9; asymmetric corruption does not approach uniformly random labels. The supplied Figure 3 text does not establish perfect fitting.
Comparisons with and without weight decay, dropout, and augmentation that establish both random-label fitting and clean-label generalization.
Separate learning trajectories for real-label patterns and corrupted labels. Aggregate training/test curves and late overfitting do not identify which labels are learned first.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted numerical values match the supplied tables; uncertainties are standard errors across five runs. Row states remain cannot_determine for the compound V4 effect because test accuracy cannot establish perfect training fit. The supports verdicts apply only to its measured degradation component. Figure 3 is already declared in rows_left_out, so it is not a missing extraction; no numerical curve values can be recovered from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random training labels or corresponding training error and test error at chance are reported.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed against clean-label training is reported.
No shuffled-pixel or Gaussian-noise inputs are tested.

The paper reports test accuracy over noise rates up to 0.9 symmetric and 0.5 asymmetric, but does not provide extractable numerical training accuracy for the same conditions or test the all-random endpoint. The training-accuracy curve for asymmetric noise r=0.4 is figure-only.
No random-label experiments compare weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation with their removal.
The paper does not test whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

relationships.condition: Conventional cross entropy on CIFAR-10 with symmetric random replacement, r=0 through 0.9; test-degradation component only.
relationships.reason: R1–R6 show test accuracy falling monotonically from 91.84% to 45.85%; this supports degradation with corruption, while perfect training fit and the chance endpoint remain untested.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy declined monotonically from 91.84% to 45.85% as symmetric replacement increased.

relationships.condition: Conventional cross entropy on CIFAR-10 with structured asymmetric corruption, r=0.1 through 0.5; test-degradation component only.
relationships.reason: R7–R11 show test accuracy falling monotonically from 91.04% to 77.48%; this supports degradation in this corruption setting without establishing perfect training fit or a chance endpoint.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy declined monotonically from 91.04% to 77.48% as asymmetric corruption increased.
